cim: Opinion AI makes answers easier to find. What we do with them may matter more.
cim_eredeti: Opinion AI makes answers easier to find. What we do with them may matter more.
szoveg_eredeti:
We are living through one of the most consequential times in all of history. Right now. Your great-great-grandkids will study the Industrial Revolution, the French Revolution, the back-to-back World War Championships that we won, and the digital revolution that came with microprocessors and the internet. They will also study the period we are living through. the next revolution: the Intelligence Revolution.

See, those who live through consequential times in history rarely know it at the time. As Kierkegaard once said, “Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.” Psychologist Robert Sternberg proposed a theory that distinguishes three kinds of intelligence: analytical, creative, and practical. It’s a useful framework for thinking about where we are. Analytical intelligence helps us examine information critically and reason through a solution. Much of our approach to academia is based on this principle. Creative intelligence helps us imagine new possibilities. Like the genius who put wheels on suitcases or pineapple on pizza. Practical intelligence is knowing how to change a tire or get the Christmas tree up without getting a divorce. By the way, there is nothing in the Bible requiring you to cut down a tree and drag it into your home. I’ve looked.

For much of human history, being “smart” was creative and practical: finding or growing food, keeping the wives and kids alive through winter, etc. Knowing how to kill a wooly mammoth wasn’t helpful unless you could actually do it. Reading tracks, anticipating an animal’s movements, and making a decision to attack at the right moment meant the difference between starving and eating. Or maybe being eaten. A farmer had to know his soil, predict the weather and fix things that broke.

Again, there wasn’t much value in knowing the answer if you couldn’t put it on the table. More recently, the smartest kids were rewarded for analytical intelligence. Think math, science, etc. These are the whiz kids who get excited about the annual Harvard-Yale rowing regatta. These are the people who can explain international monetary policy but can’t organize a backyard cookout.

Regardless, we’ve built an impressive system for identifying them. Grades. Test scores. Degrees. Credentials. We’ve gotten pretty good at measuring whether somebody can solve a problem on paper. Whether they can explain the answer or get six people to agree on it is another question.

Analytical intelligence will always matter. But, increasingly, artificial intelligence can perform analytical tasks faster than we can. Students today are questioning why they need to go to the trouble. They have a point, although outsourcing your homework isn’t quite the same as getting an education.

As Dana Hermanson, a professor at Kennesaw State University, recently wrote, “Traditional methods of teaching and assessing learning may be gone. Even the university research realm will be transformed.” That ought to get the attention of anyone considering a career in higher ed.

So if analytical answers become easier to obtain, what will become more valuable? How will we measure our students and job applicants? Nobody knows, but I suspect creative and practical intelligence are about to ask someone to hold their beer.

See, the advantage may shift away from those who know how to get the answer and towards those who know what to do with the answer. Fortune may favor the employee who can quickly find the answer, develop a relationship, explain the solution, and deliver what was promised.

ChatGPT might help you plan the perfect backyard cookout. But somebody still has to invite the neighbors, man the grill, and talk to the neighbor with the weird kids. Yes, the extroverts are about to have a moment.

The ability to find an answer may become less valuable than the ability to do something useful with it. I suspect we’ll continue to value analytical, creative, and practical intelligence. But we may become a little more careful about whom we call the smartest person in the room.

prioritas.indok: Általános véleménycikk az MI koráról konkrét hírérték és újdonság nélkül.
prioritas.cim_hu: Az MI megkönnyíti a válaszok megtalálását, de a használata a lényeg
prioritas.lead_hu: Egy véleménycikk szerint az intelligenciaforradalom küszöbén állunk, ám a technológia valódi értékét az határozza meg, hogy mire használjuk az elért tudást.
